catalog_quote: In Lelepa, stress is best described using moraic theory (Hayes 1995). ... Syllables can be light or heavy, with light syllables containing a single mora and heavy syllables containing more than one mora. While onsets do not count as morae, syllable nuclei and codas do. Light syllables are open and their nucleus is filled by a short vowel. In contrast, heavy syllables can be open or closed. ... As stress is attracted to the penultimate mora, it is not relevant to distinguish between different types of heavy syllables. In Lelepa, stress is not contrastive and the language has several predictable stress patterns, with penultimate stress the predominant pattern. 2.4.3.2 Dominant stress pattern In this pattern, stress falls on the penultimate mora. audit.reasoning: Quote, locator and page mapping all verified verbatim in the held Lacrampe 2014 thesis (sect. 2.4.3, printed pp.58-64 = PDF 86-92). The classification (weight-sensitive, right edge, stress on syllable containing the penultimate mora, heavy = CVV+CVC, secondary stress two morae leftward, listed exceptions) matches the source text and its example sets (110)-(121). The deciding source is the sole reference grammar of the language, by its principal fieldworker, with an explicit moraic analysis; Glottolog lists nothing better, and the three additional open ANU items downloaded now (Lacrampe 2012 ALS paper; Yang 2023 and Sun 2023 MA theses) all restate the same penultimate-mora rule and add only acoustic-correlate detail, not a different placement analysis. no reclassification or re-read needed.

sources.quote: 'In Lelepa, primary stress typically falls on the penultimate syllable or on the final syllable if it is a heavy syllable (Lacrampe, 2014, p. 59). Heavy syllables in Lelepa can be either open or closed.' Sect. 3.4: 'primary stress in Lelepa is predictable and it usually occurs on the penultimate syllable, unless the final syllable is heavy and attracts stress'; fn.9 restates secondary stress every second mora leftward in 4+-syllable words.
